chunks: "The standard solution is a two-stage regulator: a buck converter takes the big drop efficiently, down to just above the target, and a low-noise LDO takes the last few hundred millivolts and cleans the output.
For example 12 volts to a clean 3. 3 volts at an amp. An LDO alone would be 27 percent efficient and burn 8. 7 watts.
A buck alone is 92 percent efficient but has maybe tens of millivolts of ripple at its switching frequency. So I set the buck to about 3. 6 volts and follow it with an LDO to 3.
3. The LDO only drops 0. 3 volts, so it dissipates 0. 3 watts, and the chain is around 84 percent efficient, with the LDO rejecting the ripple. The design choice is the headroom.
Less headroom is more efficient, but PSRR gets worse as you approach dropout, so I pick the smallest headroom where the datasheet PSRR at the switching frequency still meets my noise budget.
If one LDO isn't enough, I add an LC or ferrite filter between them.
Other options are a low-noise buck, a tracking pre-regulator that sets its own headroom, and for tiny currents just an RC filter.
And I'd keep the layout separate and the hot loop small."
